lesson: Weight clues were real but weak: the strongest legal_latin MLP scan hit only 0.094–0.117 attribution, and every screened part missed the 0.15 target-drop threshold (best legal_latin drop 0.235 was still paired with held-out failure).

Late heads/MLPs often encoded broad completion or formatting, not the skill itself: layer 31 unit 6961 suppressed newline/EOS (-0.61/-0.30) and 12408 favored token starts like "Nr" and Roman numerals (0.116/0.107), but the pair still failed with only 0.170 legal_latin drop and 0.180 control change.

Single-token legal-lexical directions were the most predictive yet still nonselective: for negligence_elements, layer 22 unit 1411 aligned with "duty" at 0.410 and 9622 with "damages" at 0.283, but the screen only dropped the target by 0.044 and held-out failed.

Some apparently strong legal cues were actually generic or cross-skill: layer 18 head 17 gave a 0.189 negligence drop, but it also moved bill_of_rights by 0.087 and other legal skills by 0.02–0.04, so it was not selective enough.

The best-looking isolated parts were often no better than random: layer 24 MLP unit 6711 had 0.0 negligence_elements drop, exactly matching a random same-size part, so weight attribution alone is not enough without selective ablation.

Future runs should prioritize parts with both high attribution and task-specific readouts, then filter by held-out and control stability: many candidates exceeded 0.10 target drop, but matched controls still shifted by 0.096–0.190 and caused collateral drops like legal_terms 0.121–0.313 or contract_formation 0.102–0.315.
